sections.text: Two words you will meet a lot. A crate is the smallest unit of code the compiler builds at once. A package is a folder that Cargo manages; it holds one or more crates, plus a file called Cargo.toml that describes them.

There are two kinds of crate. A binary crate compiles to a program you can run, and it has a main function. A library crate has no main; it offers code for other crates to use. Every program in this course so far was a binary crate in a single file.
Run cargo new my_app and Cargo makes this package for you:

sections.code:
my_app/
    Cargo.toml        <- describes the package
    src/
        main.rs       <- the root of the binary crate
        lib.rs        <- optional: cargo new does not make it; you add it for a library crate

sections.text: src/main.rs is the crate root of the binary, and src/lib.rs, if you add it yourself, is the crate root of a library. The crate root file is where the compiler starts reading; its contents form the top-level module, crate, that you met earlier. Cargo.toml looks like this:

The [package] part gives the name, the version and the Rust edition. The [dependencies] part lists the other crates you want. Here we ask for rand, a popular crate that makes random numbers. "0.10" means any compatible 0.10.x version.

When you build, Cargo downloads rand from crates.io, the public place where people share crates, and builds it too. Then your code can write use rand::...; to use it. Cargo also writes a Cargo.lock file that records the exact versions, so everyone builds with the same ones.

Important: the editor in this app cannot download crates, and it compiles a single file with plain rustc, so there is no Cargo.toml here. Anything with a [dependencies] section is shown, not run. The standard library, std, is a crate that comes with Rust, so use std::... always works.
These are the Cargo commands you will use every day. Run them in a terminal, inside your package folder:

sections.code:
cargo new my_app      # make a new package
cargo build           # compile it
cargo run             # compile and run
cargo check           # check for errors, faster than build
cargo test            # run the tests (next lesson)
cargo add rand        # add a dependency to Cargo.toml
cargo build --release # compile with full optimizations

sections.text: Now back to modules. When a module grows, you move it to its own file. In src/main.rs, write mod garden; with a semicolon instead of a block. Rust then loads the module body from src/garden.rs. A module nested inside it, declared with pub mod vegetables; inside garden.rs, lives in src/garden/vegetables.rs.

The module tree is the same as if you had written everything inline. The paths in your code (garden::vegetables::count()) do not change, only where the text is stored. Here is the inline version, with comments showing where each part would live in files. It prints the same thing as the file version:

A package is like a recipe folder. Cargo.toml is the shopping list on the first page: it names the dish and the ingredients (crates) you need from the shop (crates.io). Cargo goes shopping for you and then cooks everything together with your own code.

Coming from Java, Go or C#: a crate is the unit Rust compiles in one go, roughly a Java module or JAR, a Go package or a .NET assembly (a Cargo package is closer to a Go module). If you know npm or PyPI, then Cargo.toml is like package.json or pyproject.toml, Cargo.lock is like package-lock.json, and crates.io is the registry. A package can have one library crate and many binary crates (extra binaries go in src/bin/). Cargo.lock is normally committed (cargo new sets this up), for libraries too. Workspaces let several packages share one lock file and one build folder. The older layout garden/mod.rs also works, but garden.rs next to a garden/ folder is the current style.

exercise.prompt: Pretend the nested module is the file src/shop/fruits.rs. main already calls shop::fruits::count(). Inside mod shop, add pub mod fruits with a function pub fn count() -> u32 that returns 5. It should print: shop is open, 5 kinds of fruit

tests.label: The program prints shop is open, 5 kinds of fruit
tests.output: shop is open, 5 kinds of fruit

tests.label: fruits can be reached through a use line

hints: The shop module needs a module nested inside it, like a folder inside a folder. Look at how formal sat inside greetings.
Inside mod shop, write pub mod fruits { ... } and put a function in it: pub fn count() -> u32 that returns 5. Both need pub, because main is outside.
main already calls the function by its full path: shop::fruits::count(). Once the module and the function exist, that line works.

quiz.question: Which file is the root of a binary crate in a package made by cargo new?
options: Cargo.toml, the file that describes the package
src/lib.rs, the file that holds the library code
src/main.rs, the file that holds main
quiz.explanation: cargo new makes src/main.rs the root of the binary crate, the file that holds main. src/lib.rs would be the root of a library crate, and Cargo.toml only describes the package.

quiz.question: What does the [dependencies] section of Cargo.toml do?
options: It lists the crates the package needs, which Cargo downloads and builds
It lists the functions the package makes public to other crates
It lists the source files that the compiler should include in the build
quiz.explanation: [dependencies] lists the crates the package needs, and Cargo downloads and builds them. What a crate makes public is decided with pub in the code, and the source files are found from the module tree, not from Cargo.toml.

quiz.question: In src/main.rs you write mod garden; with a semicolon. Where does Rust look for the body of that module?
options: In src/main.rs, further down below the mod line
In a file named garden.rs inside the src folder
quiz.explanation: mod garden; with a semicolon tells Rust to load the module's body from another file, garden.rs next to main.rs in src. (garden/mod.rs also works.) A body written in braces would be in the same file, and Cargo.toml has nothing to do with modules.
